question.question: An incident report records the ACR manifest digest of the image that produced a faulty result. Since then, the team has moved both the production and release tags to newer images. The original manifest is still retained. Which reference should the investigator use to retrieve exactly the recorded image?

answerChoices.text: The repository reference with the recorded manifest digest
The repository reference with its current production tag
The repository reference with its current release tag

question.explanation: Use the recorded manifest digest. Moving a tag changes the image that the tag identifies, but not the identity of the retained manifest.
question.deepExplanation: Digest addressing uses registry/repository@sha256:hash. A convenient tag can be useful for following a maintained release, but the current value of either moved tag cannot identify the historical artifact reliably.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: A stable production tag identifies the image it currently references. It can intentionally follow updates, but the stem says that tag moved after the incident, so it no longer selects the recorded artifact.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: A release-looking name is still a mutable tag unless a non-reuse or locking policy protects it. This release tag explicitly moved, so its name is not evidence of the incident image.

question.question: A framework team maintains a compatible base-image release line in ACR. Dependent build tasks already track that same-registry base image. Application teams want security servicing within the release line to trigger rebuilds without editing each Dockerfile. Which base-image reference policy fits?

answerChoices.text: Pin each Dockerfile to the digest of the original unpatched base image.
Reference a never-reused tag for the original base-image build.
Reference a stable release-line tag that the framework team updates with compatible patches.

question.explanation: Maintain a stable tag for the serviced release line. Repointing that tag to a patched base image lets the tracked dependency participate in base-image-triggered rebuilds.
question.deepExplanation: Stable means a maintained release intent, not frozen content. This policy concerns build inputs; the resulting application images can still receive unique deployment tags and require deliberate production rollout.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: A digest pins exact content and is appropriate when reproducibility requires a frozen input. It does not follow the updated release-line tag and conflicts with receiving servicing without reference edits.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: A never-reused tag keeps identifying its particular build. That policy is useful for deliberate deployment selection, but a Dockerfile left on the original build does not follow later base-image servicing.

question.question: Two independent build systems can rebuild the same application commit after different base-image patches. Each system has an incrementing build ID that is unique only within that system. Operations requires a never-reused deployment tag that identifies the exact producing build. Which policy meets both requirements?

answerChoices.text: Use the application commit hash alone for every build.
Use the build-system name plus its build ID, without reusing the resulting tag.
Use the local build ID alone, without the build-system name.
Reuse a semantic release-line tag after each successful rebuild.

question.explanation: Combine the build-system identifier with that system’s unique build ID, and never reuse the combined tag. A commit alone cannot distinguish rebuilds caused by a changed base image.
question.deepExplanation: The product guidance explicitly warns that commit-only tags are semi-stable when a base image changes. Prefixing a build ID with its build system also avoids collisions between independently numbered pipelines; this remains an enforced tagging policy, not digest immutability.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: Commit tags identify source state, but the tagging article explains that a base-image update can rebuild the same commit with new image content. They do not uniquely identify the producing build in this scenario.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: A build ID supports traceability within a single producing system. The article recommends a system prefix for multiple systems; locally unique numbers can collide under the conditions given here.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: Reusing a stable release-line tag is appropriate for maintained base images. It intentionally moves the reference and cannot retain a distinct reference for every producing deployment build.

question.question: A release pipeline has selected a unique ACR tag for an image that is now serving traffic. The team wants an ACR-side safeguard for that deployed tag rather than relying only on developers to avoid reusing its name. Which action matches the documented release safeguard?

answerChoices.text: Give the deployed image an additional semantic-version tag.
Record the image’s digest in the release notes.
Set write-enabled to false for the deployed image tag.

question.explanation: Set the deployed image tag’s write-enabled attribute to false. The product guidance recommends locking deployed tags as a release-pipeline safeguard.
question.deepExplanation: Unique tagging is a naming policy, while locking applies a registry attribute to the deployed tag. This is not a claim that administrators can never change the setting or that preview cleanup features have any particular behavior.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: An image can have several tags, and semantic versions improve human readability. Adding another tag does not apply the documented write-enabled locking attribute to the deployed tag.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Recording a digest provides immutable artifact identity for traceability. It is useful during investigation but is not the registry-side deployed-tag locking operation requested here.
